messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Leilani is a 35-year-old accountant who came to treatment nearly a year after she was mugged walking from her office to the parking garage after staying late during tax season. She had heard footsteps behind her on the concrete ramp but told herself not to overreact. When a man came up close, grabbed at her bag, and shoved her, she remembers the shock of an unprepared hand on her shoulder more than the force itself. For a few seconds she was pinned awkwardly, twisted and half crouched, tasting the metallic bitterness that had risen in her mouth while he yelled and pulled at her purse. She saw his face at close range before he ran. Since then, what has stayed with her is not only fear, but a conviction that the attack says something damning about her: that it happened because of the kind of person she is, someone inattentive, weak, and easy to target. She had come to believe that the world is dangerous in a way other people fail to grasp, and that what happened was caused by the way she acted that night.

In the weeks afterward, those meanings attached themselves to ordinary moments. At work, if she heard footsteps behind her in the hallway after everyone else had left, her body tightened instantly and she would think, again, that she should have known better, should have turned sooner, should never have been alone. On the street, a glimpse of a man who resembled the offender, or even an unexpected touch from a coworker at the copy machine, could bring the same conclusion back with force: this happened because she is the sort of person bad things happen to. Those moments did not just remind her of the mugging; they seemed to confirm her belief that nowhere is truly safe.

Once triggered, Leilani would try to manage what came up by going over the event again and again, searching for the exact point at which she could have prevented it. She dwelt on what she had done wrong—why she stayed late, why she ignored the footsteps, why she did not cross back toward the building sooner. At times the distress became so intense that she deliberately tried to blank out, staring fixedly at a spreadsheet or letting herself feel as if she were floating just outside her body until the moment passed. The more certain she became that her own character and actions had caused the attack, the more relentlessly she turned these thoughts over, as if enough self-criticism might finally produce safety.

The memories themselves are strikingly sensory and hard for her to place in the past. When they come, she can taste again that metallic, sour flavor in her mouth, and her body folds into the same tense, twisted position she had been forced into on the garage floor. At the same time, the scene can feel unreal to her, “like it happened to someone else and also like it’s happening right now.” Because she sees the event as proof of her own vulnerability and of a dangerous world, these memories land not as recollections but as evidence. They sharpen her sense that danger is present and make her scan even more closely for footsteps, faces, and sudden contact.

That sense of threat now organizes much of her day. If her husband is later than expected answering a text, she quickly assumes something bad has happened. If an elevator takes too long to arrive, her chest tightens and her mind jumps to being trapped with the wrong person. Even at home, when family members tell her she is safe, she cannot fully believe them, and she notices that she is never really able to relax. In that keyed-up state, small sounds stand out with unusual force; footsteps in the apartment hallway or behind her in the office seem instantly significant. The threat she feels also drives her back into the same strategies—mental replay, self-accusation, and deliberate emotional numbing—because being constantly braced feels preferable to being caught off guard again.

Over months, these habits have tightened around each other. The more she ruminates and blanks out, the more fragmented and bodily the memories seem when they break through, and the less convinced she is that she has truly processed what happened. After a bad episode she is harsher with herself, taking the persistence of her symptoms as further proof that something is wrong with her rather than as a consequence of trauma. That in turn leaves her more certain that the world is dangerous and that she must remain on guard. Recently, a coworker came up behind her to ask a question while she was reconciling accounts; the unexpected touch on her arm made her flinch so violently that she knocked over her coffee and had to lock herself in the restroom, tasting that same bitterness and feeling her body hunch into the old position. She sought help after that incident, frightened by how quickly she disappears from herself at work and how little reassurance reaches her. What she wants most is to stop living as if the mugging is still underway, but what she fears most is that letting her guard down would prove she has learned nothing and invite it to happen again.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state that Leilani’s negative appraisals themselves lead to or heighten triggers/reminders becoming salient cues.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly convey that intrusive trauma memories cause or generate triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not clearly describe her sense of threat as leading directly to trauma memories/intrusive recollection.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette suggests threat makes small sounds seem significant, but it does not clearly link threat as causing triggers/reminders themselves within the required causal direction.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not explicitly state that her maladaptive strategies increase or intensify her sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Since then, what has stayed with her is not only fear, but a conviction that the attack says something damning about her: that it happened because of the kind of person she is, someone inattentive, weak, and easy to target. She had come to believe that the world is dangerous in a way other people fail to grasp, and that what happened was caused by the way she acted that night.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once she had settled on those conclusions, ordinary ambiguities began to catch on them; footsteps in a hallway, a man lingering near the elevator, or a hand reaching unexpectedly into her space no longer registered as neutral details but as cues her mind seized on as potentially important.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The memories themselves are strikingly sensory and hard for her to place in the past. When they come, she can taste again that metallic, sour flavor in her mouth, and her body folds into the same tense, twisted position she had been forced into on the garage floor.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After one of these episodes, she would move through the next hours finding pieces of the mugging everywhere—in the scrape of shoes on concrete, in the angle of a stranger approaching too closely, in the end of the workday when the office thinned out—as if the memory itself had taught her what to notice.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Even at home, when family members tell her she is safe, she cannot fully believe them, and she notices that she is never really able to relax.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
On evenings when that sense of danger is strongest, the scene from the garage comes back most readily, as though staying braced keeps the attack close at hand in her mind and pulls it forward without warning.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
In that keyed-up state, small sounds stand out with unusual force; footsteps in the apartment hallway or behind her in the office seem instantly significant.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Already feeling as if danger is near, she finds that almost anything can tip into a warning—the wrong pace of someone walking behind her, a figure waiting by the parking structure, the late-day emptiness of her accounting floor—so that the world feels crowded with reminders she cannot dismiss.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The threat she feels also drives her back into the same strategies—mental replay, self-accusation, and deliberate emotional numbing—because being constantly braced feels preferable to being caught off guard again.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
But these habits leave her with no chance to discover that a moment has passed safely; by repeatedly going over the attack and shutting herself down instead of remaining present, she keeps her body convinced the danger is current and has to be anticipated at all times.
<<<END>>>
